system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 2 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 40-60 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2180-04-05 08:20:00 to 2180-04-06 16:50:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of liver transplant, diabetes, and recent hernia repair was readmitted after a blood culture from a prior discharge grew gram-negative rods. He was asymptomatic but started on intravenous cefepime. Imaging with CT and MRI revealed findings suggestive of possible cholangitis related to biliary stents, which were removed via ERCP. A PICC line was placed for two weeks of outpatient antibiotic therapy. His kidney function improved during the stay, and he was discharged home with instructions to continue sirolimus and Myfortic, stop Lasix and fenofibrate pending primary care review, and follow up for transplant care and pancreatic cyst monitoring.
problems: Other specified bacterial infections in conditions classified elsewhere and of unspecified site, other gram-negative organisms
Hypertensive chronic kidney disease, unspecified, with chronic kidney disease stage I through stage IV, or unspecified
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled
Personal history of malignant neoplasm of prostate

Brief Hospital Course:
REASON FOR HOSPITAL ADMISSION:
Mr ___ is a ___ with h/o crytogenic cirrhosis, now 10 
months s/p liver transplant, also with CKD, and GERD, who 
presents with chest pain and signs of volume overload.  
.
HOSPITAL COURSE:
.  
# Chest pain: Pt presented with chest pain located at the base 
of the sternum which was constant, started at rest and unchanged 
with any kind of activity. Pt also had diffuse PR depressions in 
I, aVL, and several of the ___ leads - all of which 
had upsloping ST segments. TTE showed only very mild area of 
distal septal hypokinesis which did not correspond to EKG 
changes. The differential however included MI, but cardiac 
enzymes were negative pointing away from an ischemic event. Pt 
does have a history of GERD however symptoms were not associated 
with eating and not worse when lying down. Finally, PE was moved 
to the background as pt had a negative DDimer. It was presumed 
that the patient had a viral illness and did not manifest 
symptoms or prodrome due to immunosuppression, see cryptogenic 
cirrhosis below. ESR and CRP were mildly elevated which would 
also be consistent with pericarditis. In the setting of 
immunosuppression, other atypical infectious agents were 
considered, however pt without significant findings on chest xr 
and with dramatic resolution of his symptoms only several hours 
after admission.  Pt was given aspirin and colchicine for 
pericarditis. It was felt that given rapid clinical improvement 
prednisone was not necessary at this time. NSAIDs were avoided 
in liver transplant/CKD patient. 

.  
# Volume overload: Pt presented with lower extremity edema and 
crackles on lung exam. Recent discontinuation of lasix (40 
daily). TTE with only very mild regional hypokinesis and no 
evidence of tamponade. No evidence of diastolic dysfunction. 
Clinically, patient with lower extremity edema, bibasilar 
crackles, and elevated JVP. Lasix was administered with good 
effect, and pt was discharged back on home lasix. Transplant 
team felt that lower extremity edema was a side effect of 
sirolimus.
.  
# Crytogenic cirrhosis: Pt is s/p liver transplant ___. 
Hepatology consulted in ED, cardiology fellow discussed case 
with Dr. ___. LFTs were within normal limits. Pt was 
maintained on his home regimen of MMF, sirolimus, bactrim, and 
ursodiol.
.  
# CKD: Creatinine of 1.5 on presentation was at recent baseline. 
Medications were renally dose. NSAIDs avoided for treatment of 
pericarditis; colchicine was dosed renally. 
.  
CHRONIC ISSUES:  
# Hypertriglyceridemia: Continued home fibrates.

# Anemia: HCT was at baseline. DPt to have further workup as an 
outpatient.

# HTN: Stable, continued metoprolol tratrate 12.5 BID

microbiology.comments: CMV DNA not detected.  Performed by PCR.  Detection Range: 600 - 100,000 copies/ml.

NEGATIVE FOR CMV IgM ANTIBODY BY EIA.  INTERPRETATION:  INFECTION AT UNDETERMINED TIME.  A positive IgG result generally indicates past exposure.  Infection with CMV once contracted remains latent and may reactivate when immunity is compromised.  If current infection is suspected, submit follow-up serum in 2-3 weeks.  Greatly elevated serum protein with IgG levels >2000 mg/dl may cause  interference with CMV IgM results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with chest pain this morning. Can you tell me more about it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it started this morning. Sharp pain right here in the middle of my chest. It doesn’t move, but it hurts more when I lie down or take a deep breath. Leaning forward helps a little.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s helpful. Any nausea, sweating, or shortness of breath?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A little short of breath, but no nausea or sweating. I’ve had some swelling in my legs, but that’s been going on for a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. You’re on a number of medications, including sirolimus and Mycophenolate for your liver transplant, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and I stopped my Lasix about a month ago. The liver team told me to.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That might explain some of the swelling. We’ve reviewed your EKG, and it shows some changes—small ST elevations in leads I and aVL. That can be seen in several conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it a heart attack? I’ve been worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your cardiac enzymes—troponin—twice, and both were normal. That makes a heart attack very unlikely. We also did an echocardiogram. Your heart’s pumping well, no major wall motion issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So what is it then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Given the sharp, positional pain and the EKG changes, we think you have pericarditis— inflammation of the lining around the heart. It’s not uncommon, especially in people on immunosuppressants.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? Did something cause it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be uncomfortable, but it’s usually not dangerous. We don’t see signs of infection in your blood cultures, and your CMV tests were negative. It may be a mild viral illness that your body didn’t fully react to because of your medications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. So what’s the treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re starting you on colchicine, which helps reduce the inflammation. We’ll also keep you on aspirin. We’re avoiding NSAIDs because of your kidney function and liver transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my chest pain? It’s still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but it should improve over the next day or two. You can take Tylenol or tramadol for pain, but please don’t exceed 2,000 mg of Tylenol in a day—your liver needs to stay protected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also noticed some crackles in your lungs and your leg swelling. Your JVP is a bit high. We think you’re a little fluid overloaded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Because I stopped the Lasix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’re restarting your Lasix to help with the fluid. The transplant team also mentioned your leg swelling might be partly due to sirolimus, but managing fluid is still important.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat EKG this afternoon still shows the ST changes, but your symptoms are improving, which is a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: The pain is definitely better. I can breathe more easily now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep monitoring you. Your labs show mild inflammation—ESR and CRP are up—but no infection. Blood cultures came back clean.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need more tests? I remember last time they did a stress test.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You actually had a nuclear stress test before this admission, and it was normal—no blockages, good heart function. That helped us rule out coronary disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. What about my kidney numbers? I’ve had issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is 1.5, which is within your usual range. We’re being careful with medications—colchicine is dosed for your kidney function, and we avoided NSAIDs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The chest X-ray showed some hazy areas at the bases. Could be atelectasis or mild fluid, but nothing that suggests pneumonia. It’s likely related to your positioning or mild congestion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing to worry about?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. We’re not seeing signs of infection, and your oxygen levels are good. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. You’re doing well. Your chest pain is mostly gone, and your breathing is better. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue all your usual medications. We’re adding colchicine twice a day for four weeks to help prevent the pericarditis from coming back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the Lasix?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, back on 20 mg daily. Watch your leg swelling and let your doctor know if it gets worse. Also, keep taking your lansoprazole, sirolimus, and the others as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Any restrictions? Can I go back to my usual activities?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can resume normal activities as tolerated. Avoid heavy lifting for a few days. If the chest pain returns, or if you have trouble breathing, call your doctor or come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll see your transplant doctor soon. They’ll also coordinate your pancreatic cyst monitoring. Make sure to keep all your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad you’re feeling better. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick update—your discharge papers are ready. You’ll get prescriptions for colchicine and Lasix. The rest stay the same.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. I’ll pick them up before I leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will come by with your discharge instructions and medication list. You’re cleared to go home when you’re ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I think I’m all set. Thanks again for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take it easy, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your CMV test came back negative, so no reactivation. That’s good news for your transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We monitor it closely. You’re stable, and your liver numbers are normal. Keep up with your appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks for taking such good care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our pleasure. Take care, and feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in—how are you doing before discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Feeling good. Pain is gone, and I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Remember: colchicine twice daily, Lasix once daily, and watch for any chest pain or breathing issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll keep an eye on it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re all set. Have a safe trip home.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of liver transplant, chronic kidney disease, and GERD was admitted for substernal chest pain that improved with leaning forward and had a pleuritic component. Initial evaluation revealed sinus tachycardia, positional chest pain, and EKG changes including ST elevations in leads I and aVL, but normal troponins and echocardiogram. Pericarditis was diagnosed, likely due to a viral illness masked by immunosuppression. He was treated with colchicine and aspirin, avoiding NSAIDs due to transplant and kidney status. Volume overload from recent Lasix discontinuation was managed with diuresis. Symptoms resolved rapidly, and he was discharged home on colchicine for four weeks and restarted on Lasix, with follow-up planned for transplant and pancreatic cyst monitoring.
